M1.notes: The letter keeps the analyst title, presents note-taking and the class interview project accurately, and avoids the inflated Lumen and portfolio phrasing. The only mild stretch is 'I pushed to report it separately,' where memory says Riley only asked whether to; it is not a listed violation, so it is not flagged.

unsupported_self_claims.quote: I ran a semi-structured interview study with six students, synthesized it with affinity diagramming
unsupported_self_claims.why: Calls the User Research Methods class project an 'interview study' without saying it was a class project. Only the capstone usability test is labeled as coursework.

M2.lead_interest: How people make sense of AI features that adapt based on their personal data, and how that understanding shapes trust, reliance, and the explanations and control people need as the stakes rise.
M2.notes: The statement is accurate and grounded in the AI Coach survey story, keeps the analyst role clear, and leaves all faculty-fit content as placeholders, so it makes no claims about Prof. Li. The interest is framed somewhat more around understanding and trust than Riley's 'feel they still have a say' (agency appears only in Q3), and Q2's trust-measurement angle leans slightly toward industry framing.

REV.lead_interest: What people think is going on when an app uses their own data to make decisions for them, and what would make them feel they still have a say, with privacy treated as one facet rather than the core.
REV.notes: The claims stay inside every boundary: analyst title, note-taker role, class projects named as coursework, no publications, and the 'one in ten' figure hedged as an impression. The Li connection accurately cites T3 and T1 without claiming Riley has read her papers, but an unfilled bracketed placeholder for additional faculty remains in the draft.

M3.lead_interest: What people think is going on when an app uses their own data to decide things for them, and what would make them feel they still have a say.

unsupported_fit_claims.quote: Your COLM 2026 paper on autonomy and personalization stood out to me.
unsupported_fit_claims.why: Riley has not read Prof. Li's papers. Saying a specific paper 'stood out' implies Riley read it, which is unsupported unless confirmed in session.

faculty_misdescriptions.quote: and reduced the trust costs of personalization
faculty_misdescriptions.why: The snapshot records only that risk-contingent autonomy improves perceived control. The specific claim about reduced trust costs is an extrapolated result not in the ground truth.

M3.notes: The email accurately frames Riley as an analyst and note-taker, keeps the interest on agency and understanding rather than privacy, and closely mirrors the voice sample. The 'about one in ten' figure is stated loosely, not as a precise statistic, so it was not flagged. Its only risks are the implied reading of the COLM paper and a slightly extended description of that paper's findings.

REV_first.lead_interest: How people make sense of products that quietly adapt to them using their personal data: what theories they form when the system doesn't explain itself, when those theories are wrong, and how that affects trust and reliance, especially as stakes rise.
REV_first.notes: The draft accurately represents Riley's analyst role, note-taking, class projects, and lack of publications, and it ties the AI Coach survey cluster to Prof. Li's T3 autonomy/personalization work without a privacy reframing. It emphasizes trust and mental models more than 'having a say' and leaves several placeholders, but its tone ('a reasonable choice for the product') closely mirrors Riley's voice.

cross_material_inconsistencies: Minor count discrepancy: REV says "A couple had turned off health-data sharing" while M3 says "A few turned off health-data sharing."
cross.revision_change_summary: REV reframes the statement away from a skills-and-metrics job-application pitch (A/B test ownership, SRM debugging, bootstrap CIs) toward a personal narrative about users' understanding of, and sense of say over, apps that act on their personal data, explicitly disavowing engagement optimization ("I don't want to study how to make people engage more") and adding privacy and agency.
